title: Wine experts called white wine red

angle.point: What we see decides what we smell, proven when enology students described a dyed white wine with red-wine words.
angle.stakes: Fifty-four wine undergraduates whose studies relied on their highly trained noses.
angle.turn: They smelled a white wine dyed red and mapped their red-wine words onto it.
angle.takeaway: Our visual expectations can completely overwrite our sense of smell.

beats.voiceover: Wine students called white wine red.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: In 2001, fifty-four wine undergraduates in Bordeaux wrote down smell words for a real white and a real red wine.

elements.text: 54 undergraduates from the Bordeaux enology faculty.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: A week later, the researcher gave them that same white wine, plus a glass of it dyed red with an odorless grape pigment.

elements.text: White wine colored with natural grape anthocyanins.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: When they smelled the fake red, they described it using the exact red-wine words they had used the week before.

elements.text: Described as a red wine by a panel of 54 tasters.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: Their eyes completely overwrote what their noses were telling them. No way. Really.

claims.claim: In 2001, 54 wine undergraduates in Bordeaux took part in a test.
The students built a personal list of smell words for a real white and a real red wine.
A week later, they were given the same white wine and a version dyed red with an odorless grape pigment (anthocyanins).
The tasters described the dyed white wine using red-wine words.
The visual information caused the tasters to discount the olfactory information.

publish.title: Wine experts called white wine red
publish.description: In 2001, a simple test proved that what we see completely overwrites what we smell. Fifty-four wine students were fooled by a tasteless dye.
